title: Restoring damaged paintings
paragraphs: Conservators who restore damaged paintings face a dilemma: how much of the missing work should be filled in? A restoration that is too bold risks replacing the artist's intention with the restorer's guess, while one that is too timid leaves visible gaps that distract viewers from the work as a whole. Many museums now favor a compromise in which new paint is applied only where the original design is certain, and in a form that can be distinguished on close inspection yet disappears at normal viewing distance. Critics of this approach argue that it flatters the viewer, who is offered an illusion of wholeness while the loss itself goes unacknowledged. Supporters reply that the technique is honest precisely because it can be detected by anyone who looks closely.
